outline.description: A concise summary of the entire survey paper. It will outline the rapid evolution of LLM security threats from 2023 to 2026, covering training-time vulnerabilities (data and model poisoning), inference-time exploits (adversarial attacks and prompt injection), and output reliability issues (hallucinations). The abstract will highlight the paradigm shift from simple text-based exploits to complex vulnerabilities in autonomous agents and Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), summarizing key defense strategies and future directions.

outline.title: 1. Introduction
outline.description: This section introduces the motivation and scope of the survey, detailing the rapid and sophisticated evolution of the LLM security landscape between 2023 and 2026. It will outline the transition from early prompt-based exploits and basic factual errors to deep architectural vulnerabilities, autonomous agent weaponization, and reasoning-level poisoning. The introduction will clearly define the scope of the survey, summarizing the contributions and providing a roadmap for the subsequent sections, emphasizing the critical need for robust alignment and defense mechanisms in both standard LLMs and emerging Large Reasoning Models (LRMs).

outline.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: This section establishes the foundational concepts and terminology used throughout the survey. It will define key terms such as Jailbreak, Prompt Injection (Direct vs. Indirect), Attack Success Rate (ASR), Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO), and Hallucination. Furthermore, it will provide a brief overview of LLM architectures, including the recent emergence of Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). Finally, it will present a comprehensive threat model overview, distinguishing between training-time threats (e.g., poisoning) and inference-time threats (e.g., adversarial attacks, prompt injection).

outline.title: 3. Data and Model Poisoning: Training-Time Vulnerabilities
outline.description: This section covers the evolution of data and model poisoning from 2023 to 2026. It will begin with early 2024 research demonstrating the fragility of RLHF and DPO, specifically how preference datasets can be manipulated via label-flipping to compromise reward models [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF, Kusaka_2025_LLM]. It will explore the expansion of poisoning into specialized domains like code generation [Yan_2024_LLM, Hossen_2024_Double] and multilingual contexts where backdoors transfer across languages [He_2024_LLMs]. Crucially, it will detail the 2025 paradigm shift toward 'behavioral' and 'reasoning' poisoning in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), demonstrating how the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process can be hijacked to induce deceptive reasoning or force logical step-skipping [Zhu_2025_Think, Shen_2025_Decepchain].

outline.title: 4. Adversarial Attacks on LLMs
outline.description: This section details the progression of adversarial attacks from simple exploits to deep architectural vulnerabilities. It will start with foundational 2023 work on targeted data poisoning in natural language-to-code generators via 'reverse code repair' [Improta_2023_AI]. It will then cover 2024 advancements in white-box analysis tools measuring backdoor triggers in neuron activations and embeddings [Cheng_2024_Unit, Hussain_2024_Measuring, Nguyen_2024_Pbp]. The section will also address interaction-based vulnerabilities exploiting multi-turn conversational history [Hao_2024_Exploring] and 'context-shifting' strategies bypassing guardrails via expert programming contexts [Noever_2024_AI]. Finally, it will highlight 2025 trends focusing on autonomous agents, specifically the susceptibility of the ReAct framework to control-flow hijacking and autonomous CVE exploitation.

outline.title: 5. Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: This section explores the rapid evolution of prompt injection (PI) and jailbreaking between 2024 and 2026. It will discuss early 2024 structural and formatting vulnerabilities, such as 'FlipAttack' [Liu_2024_Flipattack] and 'AutoDan' [Liu_2024_Autodan], which exploited autoregressive properties, alongside automated black-box generation frameworks using evolutionary algorithms [Zhao_2024_SQL]. The narrative will then shift to the 2025 paradigm shift toward complex, autonomous agentic systems, investigating Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in multi-modal environments like web navigation and coding editors [Shi_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_Webinject, Johnson_2025_LLM]. Furthermore, it will analyze new vulnerabilities introduced by 'Reasoning LLMs' (RLLMs) like DeepSeek-R1, specifically targeting their internal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes [Cui_2025_LLM, Cui_2025_LLMs].

outline.title: 6. LLM Hallucinations and Factual Inconsistencies
outline.description: This section examines the transition from basic factual error detection to deep mechanistic auditing of LLM hallucinations (2024-2026). It will cover 2024 foundational work on visual hallucinations in Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), specifically the 'language prior' problem [Wang_2024_Mllm, Xing_2024_Mitigating], and the rise of Natural Language Inference (NLI) for factual consistency checking [Jing_2024_Scale, Zhang_2024_Comparative]. The section will highlight 2025 advancements demonstrating that specialized small-scale models (3.8B to 8B parameters) can match or exceed GPT-4 in hallucination detection [Ivry_2025_Paladin, Yaron_2025_GPT, Paudel_2025_Hallucinot]. It will also explore the expansion into multilingual contexts [Islam_2025_LLMs, Tang_2025_Mitigating] and specialized domains such as climate science [Thulke_2025_Listen].

outline.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms across the identified threat categories. It will synthesize how the field is moving from simple prompt engineering to internal activation monitoring and robust alignment techniques. Topics will include mitigating the 'language prior' in MLLMs to reduce visual hallucinations [Xing_2024_Mitigating], defending against Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in agentic workflows, and securing the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes in Large Reasoning Models against behavioral poisoning. The section will evaluate the trade-offs between security guardrails, perplexity filters, and model utility.

outline.title: 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: A MANDATORY dedicated section covering the benchmarks, datasets, metrics, tools, and evaluation frameworks utilized across all four threat categories. It will detail how Attack Success Rate (ASR) is measured for prompt injection and jailbreaks, the use of Natural Language Inference (NLI) paradigms for evaluating hallucinations [Jing_2024_Scale, Zhang_2024_Comparative], and the deployment of white-box analysis tools to measure backdoor triggers in neuron activations [Cheng_2024_Unit, Hussain_2024_Measuring]. The section will also discuss the challenges of evaluating autonomous agents and Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs), emphasizing the need for dynamic, multi-turn evaluation frameworks rather than static single-turn benchmarks.

outline.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section synthesizes the gaps, limitations, and future directions in LLM security research. It will discuss the ongoing arms race between automated black-box jailbreaks and dynamic defense mechanisms. A major focus will be the unresolved challenges in securing autonomous agentic systems and the inherent vulnerabilities of the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning processes in emerging RLLMs. The discussion will also highlight the difficulty of achieving robust multilingual alignment and the persistent threat of data poisoning in the model supply chain.

outline.title: 10. Conclusion
outline.description: The conclusion will provide a final synthesis of the survey, reiterating the critical shift from static, text-based vulnerabilities to dynamic, agentic, and reasoning-based threats. It will offer practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners, emphasizing the necessity of defense-in-depth strategies, specialized small-scale models for auditing, and the urgent need for standardized, multi-turn evaluation frameworks to ensure the safe deployment of next-generation LLMs.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.text: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into critical infrastructure, healthcare, finance, and consumer applications has precipitated a fundamental paradigm shift in artificial intelligence security. As these models become increasingly ubiquitous and autonomous, they introduce novel attack vectors that threaten system integrity, data privacy, and user safety. This survey presents a comprehensive examination of the contemporary LLM security landscape. Through a systematic literature review of 129 recent studies, this paper categorizes and analyzes the multifaceted threat models inherent in modern generative AI systems. The analysis systematically explores four primary vulnerability domains: training-time data and model poisoning, sophisticated adversarial attacks, prompt injection and jailbreaking mechanisms, and the pervasive issue of LLM hallucinations and factual inconsistencies. Key findings indicate a rapid evolution in the threat landscape, transitioning from rudimentary prompt-based exploits to complex, architecturally embedded vulnerabilities, thereby highlighting the inadequacy of traditional, single-layer security paradigms. To address these emerging threats, the survey synthesizes significant practical contributions to the field. It evaluates advanced testing methodologies and comprehensive evaluation frameworks that represent a necessary paradigm shift in how AI vulnerabilities are assessed. Furthermore, the paper details cross-cutting defense mechanisms and mitigation strategies, emphasizing the critical need for robust, multi-layered security architectures rather than localized patches. By consolidating current knowledge, identifying critical gaps in existing defenses, and outlining open challenges, this survey provides researchers and software engineering practitioners with a foundational roadmap for developing secure, resilient, and trustworthy large language models.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.text:
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) into critical infrastructure, healthcare, finance, and everyday consumer applications has precipitated a profound paradigm shift in the cybersecurity landscape. Historically, information security has focused on deterministic vulnerabilities within software systems—such as buffer overflows, cross-site scripting, and SQL injections—where the logic is explicitly programmed and flaws can be patched through code revisions. However, the advent of deep learning and, more recently, Large Language Models (LLMs), has introduced a fundamentally different class of vulnerabilities. AI systems are not programmed but trained; their behavior emerges from complex, high-dimensional statistical representations learned from vast datasets [Bender_2021_Stochastic]. 

This shift from deterministic logic to probabilistic inference has given rise to AI-specific security threats. In this new paradigm, adversaries do not necessarily exploit traditional software bugs; instead, they manipulate the inputs or the training data to subvert the model's intended behavior. The opacity of deep neural networks exacerbates this issue, making it exceedingly difficult to guarantee robustness or interpret the root causes of failures [Bommasani_2021_Foundation]. Consequently, securing AI systems requires a departure from conventional cybersecurity frameworks, demanding novel methodologies that address the inherent vulnerabilities of statistical learning models.

As AI technologies have advanced, the threat landscape has evolved in tandem, growing in both complexity and scale. Early research in adversarial machine learning primarily concentrated on the computer vision domain, demonstrating how imperceptible perturbations to images could cause state-of-the-art classifiers to make glaring errors [Goodfellow_2014_Explaining]. Techniques such as the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) established the foundational understanding of evasion attacks. However, the threat landscape has since expanded far beyond simple image classification. The discrete nature of text makes gradient-based optimization more challenging, yet attackers have successfully adapted these principles to natural language, developing sophisticated token-manipulation strategies that force LLMs into unintended states [Zou_2023_Universal].

With the proliferation of generative AI and LLMs, adversaries have developed sophisticated techniques tailored specifically to natural language and code generation. Modern language models, despite being equipped with safety mechanisms and guardrails such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), remain highly susceptible to novel attack vectors [Ouyang_2022_Training]. For instance, recent studies have demonstrated that these defenses can be easily circumvented through jailbreaking strategies, utilizing carefully crafted prompts that exploit model vulnerabilities to elicit malicious or restricted outputs [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. Furthermore, the deployment of LLMs as coding assistants and autonomous agents has introduced critical security risks. Attackers can leverage these systems to generate malicious payloads or bypass traditional guardrails by embedding contextual cues that trick the model into compliance [Noever_2024_AI]. Prompt injection, where untrusted user input overrides the developer's system instructions, has emerged as a primary vector for compromising LLM-integrated applications, allowing attackers to hijack agentic workflows and exfiltrate sensitive data [Greshake_2023_NotWhat].

Beyond inference-time exploits, the foundational training and fine-tuning phases of LLMs present massive attack surfaces. Data and model poisoning attacks have evolved from simple label-flipping to sophisticated backdoor insertions, where adversaries inject latent triggers into the vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the internet [Carlini_2023_Poisoning]. When activated by a specific prompt, these backdoors can hijack the model's output, posing severe risks to downstream applications. Concurrently, the inherent tendency of LLMs to generate plausible but factually incorrect information—termed hallucinations—has transitioned from a mere reliability issue to a critical security vulnerability. Attackers have begun weaponizing hallucinations, such as through "package hallucination" attacks, where models invent non-existent software libraries that attackers subsequently register on public repositories to execute supply chain attacks [Ji_2023_Survey].

The period between 2023 and 2026 has witnessed an unprecedented arms race between AI developers and adversaries. While early LLM security research focused on static, text-based vulnerabilities, the current landscape is characterized by dynamic, multi-turn, and agentic exploits. Existing surveys have provided valuable snapshots of the field; however, the rapid pace of innovation necessitates a comprehensive, up-to-date synthesis that captures the transition from basic exploits to deep architectural vulnerabilities and mechanistic auditing [Wang_2024_Security]. There is a critical need to systematize the fragmented literature, connecting the underlying mechanisms of data poisoning, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and hallucinations with state-of-the-art testing methodologies and defensive frameworks.

To address this gap, this survey provides a holistic and structured analysis of the LLM security landscape, spanning the critical evolutionary period from 2019 to 2026, with a specific emphasis on the rapid advancements observed between 2023 and 2026. The primary contributions of this paper are fourfold:
1. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of LLM vulnerabilities, detailing the mechanistic evolution of threats across the entire model lifecycle, from training-time poisoning to inference-time jailbreaking.
2. We critically analyze the intersection of reliability and security, specifically examining how phenomena like LLM hallucinations are weaponized by adversaries to facilitate broader systemic attacks.
3. We provide a dedicated, in-depth evaluation of testing methodologies, benchmarks, metrics, and red-teaming frameworks essential for rigorously assessing LLM robustness.
4. We synthesize cross-cutting defense strategies and identify critical open challenges, offering a strategic roadmap for future research in secure AI development.

The remainder of this survey is organized as follows. Section 2 establishes the background and preliminaries, defining the core concepts and terminology utilized throughout the paper. Section 3 explores training-time vulnerabilities, detailing the evolution of data and model poisoning attacks. Section 4 examines the progression of adversarial attacks on LLMs, tracing the shift from simple token manipulation to deep architectural exploits. Section 5 investigates the rapid evolution of prompt injection and jailbreaking techniques. Section 6 analyzes LLM hallucinations and factual inconsistencies through a security lens. Section 7 provides a dedicated overview of the testing methodologies, benchmarks, and evaluation frameworks used to measure LLM security. Section 8 synthesizes cross-cutting defenses and mitigation strategies across all identified threat categories. Section 9 discusses open challenges and future research directions. Finally, Section 10 concludes the survey, reiterating the critical paradigm shifts in the LLM security landscape and summarizing key takeaways.

conclusion.title: Conclusion and Future Work
conclusion.text:
The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into critical infrastructure, software engineering workflows, and autonomous systems has precipitated a fundamental paradigm shift in cybersecurity. This survey has systematically mapped the expansive and rapidly evolving LLM threat landscape, spanning from foundational training-time vulnerabilities to complex inference-time exploits. Our analysis reveals that as models grow in capability, modality, and autonomy, their attack surfaces expand commensurately. Training-time threats, notably data poisoning and stealthy backdoor injections, have demonstrated that critical vulnerabilities can be deeply embedded within model weights long before deployment. Concurrently, inference-time threats—ranging from prompt injection and jailbreaking to adversarial perturbations—have exposed the fragility of current safety alignment techniques. Furthermore, the persistent challenge of hallucinations continues to undermine the factual integrity of LLM outputs, posing severe risks in high-stakes domains.

A critical trend identified across the literature is the escalating sophistication of adversarial methodologies. Between 2023 and 2026, the threat landscape transitioned from rudimentary, single-turn prompt exploits to highly complex, multi-turn, and agentic attack vectors. Adversaries no longer merely target surface-level outputs; they exploit the internal mechanics, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, and tool-use capabilities of autonomous AI agents. Similarly, adversarial attacks have expanded beyond unimodal text to encompass multimodal vulnerabilities, where malicious instructions are embedded within images or audio, bypassing traditional text-based guardrails. This evolution underscores a persistent arms race between model capabilities and adversarial ingenuity, shifting the focus from static vulnerabilities to dynamic, procedural exploits.

The practical implications of these findings for LLM deployment are profound. The historical reliance on localized, single-layer defenses—such as static input filtering or basic reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)—is demonstrably insufficient against modern, adaptive threats. As LLMs are increasingly embedded into financial systems, healthcare diagnostics, and automated code generation, the potential blast radius of a successful exploit grows exponentially. Consequently, organizations must adopt a "defense-in-depth" posture. This requires implementing cross-cutting mitigation strategies that integrate robust data provenance tracking during training, dynamic input and output sanitization at inference, and continuous runtime monitoring to detect anomalous or malicious model behavior.

Despite significant advancements in AI security, several critical open challenges remain. First, the inherent tension between model utility and safety alignment continues to confound researchers; overly stringent guardrails frequently degrade performance and reasoning capabilities, while permissive models remain highly vulnerable to jailbreaking. Second, the evaluation of LLM security is currently hindered by a reliance on static benchmarks, which fail to capture the dynamic, interactive nature of modern agentic exploits. The lack of standardized, scalable, and multi-turn evaluation frameworks prevents a comprehensive assessment of model robustness. Finally, eradicating hallucinations and ensuring factual consistency, particularly in specialized domains like code generation and medical diagnosis, remains an unsolved problem, complicated by the opaque nature of LLM reasoning processes and the limitations of current fact-checking mechanisms.

Addressing these challenges necessitates a concerted effort in several future research directions. Future work must prioritize the development of dynamic, automated red-teaming frameworks capable of simulating sophisticated, multi-agent adversarial scenarios. Additionally, research into mechanistic interpretability is crucial for understanding how vulnerabilities manifest within neural architectures. Advancements in this area could enable the surgical removal of backdoors or the targeted unlearning of harmful behaviors without necessitating computationally expensive full-model retraining. Furthermore, as multimodal and autonomous systems proliferate, developing cross-modal defense mechanisms and verifiable safety constraints for agentic actions—ensuring that models cannot execute destructive commands even if successfully compromised—will be paramount.

Based on the comprehensive analysis presented in this survey, we offer actionable recommendations for both practitioners and researchers. For practitioners deploying LLMs, it is imperative to implement multi-layered guardrails, enforce strict principle-of-least-privilege access controls for autonomous agents, and establish continuous, automated security auditing pipelines. Practitioners should operate under the "assume breach" paradigm, designing system architectures that fail safely even when the underlying LLM is compromised. For the research community, we recommend shifting focus from static vulnerability discovery to the development of resilient, self-healing model architectures. Researchers should collaborate to establish standardized, open-source dynamic testing environments that accurately reflect real-world, multi-turn adversarial interactions, thereby closing the gap between theoretical vulnerabilities and practical security.

Ultimately, securing Large Language Models is not a static objective but a continuous, dynamic imperative. As AI systems become increasingly autonomous and deeply woven into the fabric of digital infrastructure, ensuring their security, reliability, and alignment with human intent is arguably the most critical challenge of the modern technological era. Only through rigorous, cross-disciplinary collaboration and the proactive development of comprehensive, multi-layered defense strategies can the full transformative potential of LLMs be safely and sustainably realized.

adversarial_attacks.title: Adversarial Attacks and Jailbreaking Mechanisms
adversarial_attacks.text:
## Adversarial Attacks and Jailbreaking Mechanisms

The landscape of adversarial attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) has transitioned from rudimentary prompt-based exploits to sophisticated architectural and procedural vulnerabilities. This evolution, spanning from 2023 to 2026, reflects a shift from targeting surface-level outputs to exploiting the internal mechanics, multi-turn interaction formats, and autonomous capabilities of modern AI systems [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5]. Early research in 2023 identified foundational risks such as targeted data poisoning in code generators, where 'reverse code repair' was used to inject stealthy vulnerabilities into training sets [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5]. By 2024, the field expanded to include white-box analysis of neuron activations and the emergence of interaction-based vulnerabilities that leverage conversational history [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5]. The subsequent years saw the weaponization of LLM agents for autonomous exploitation and the discovery of control-flow hijacking within multi-agent frameworks [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5, Triedman_2025_Multi].

### White-box Analysis of Internal Mechanics

As adversarial strategies matured, researchers moved beyond black-box testing to conduct white-box analyses of the internal manifestations of attacks. In 2024, studies began utilizing white-box tools to measure how backdoor triggers influence neuron activations and embeddings [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v5]. A prominent example is the analysis of CodeBERT, where researchers identified internal backdoor signals through model parameters and activations [Hussain_2024_Measuring]. This investigation revealed that activation values of poisoned samples tend to group into a single cluster within the upper encoder layers (specifically L6-L11) of a compromised model, whereas clean samples remain scattered [Hussain_2024_Measuring].

Methodologically, this white-box approach involves comparing clean and poisoned models fine-tuned on datasets like Devign for defect detection [Hussain_2024_Measuring]. Techniques such as Gaussian kernel density estimation are employed to compare the distribution of attention weights and biases, while layer-wise k-means clustering is applied to high-dimensional activation vectors [Hussain_2024_Measuring]. Furthermore, visualization of [CLS] token context embeddings using t-SNE has demonstrated that poisoned samples form distinct clusters based on trigger types [Hussain_2024_Measuring]. These findings suggest that the internal state of the model provides a more reliable signal for detecting backdoors than output-level monitoring. Mitigation strategies explored in this context include weight-resetting experiments, where fine-tuned weights that deviate significantly from pre-trained weights are reverted to their original state [Hussain_2024_Measuring].

### Context-Shifting and Jailbreaking Strategies

Jailbreaking mechanisms have evolved to exploit the 'generalization mismatch' between safety training and the complex contexts in which LLMs operate [Cheng_2024_LLM]. A primary technique is 'context-shifting,' where malicious requests are embedded within expert programming or technical environments to bypass standard safety guardrails [Noever_2024_AI]. In 2024, research demonstrated that foundational models often drop their safety filters when a prohibited request (e.g., designing a ransomware delivery system) is reframed as a technical coding challenge or an API setup request [Noever_2024_AI]. This vulnerability allows LLMs to act as recommender systems for malicious software supply chain endpoints, including compromised GitHub repositories, malicious NPM packages, and typo-squatted libraries [Noever_2024_AI].

Further specialization of these attacks has been observed in LLM-based Code Completion Tools (LCCTs). These tools are susceptible to 'Contextual Information Aggregation Attacks,' which exploit multi-file context features [Cheng_2024_LLM]. For instance, a 'Filename Proxy Attack' involves renaming a file to a sensitive query to trigger completion, while 'Cross-File Attacks' encode sensitive responses in one file to be called by another [Cheng_2024_LLM]. Additionally, 'Hierarchical Code Exploitation Attacks' obscure malicious intent by distributing queries across multiple variables or using string concatenation within code snippets [Cheng_2024_LLM].

In 2025, the CodeJailbreaker framework introduced a method to bypass safety mechanisms by implicitly encoding malicious intent within simulated software commit messages [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. By framing the model as a software maintainer and presenting malicious functionality as a 'fix' or 'feature update' in a commit message, attackers can elicit harmful code generation [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. This approach highlights a critical gap in safety alignment, where models prioritize instruction-following in technical contexts over safety constraints [Ouyang_2025_LLM].

### Multi-turn Conversational Exploits

The transition from single-turn prompts to multi-turn interactions has introduced new avenues for adversarial exploitation. The flexible multi-turn format increases the complexity of trigger designs and amplifies the vulnerability of chat models [Hao_2024_Exploring]. In 2024, the 'Distributed Triggers-based Backdoor Attacking' framework was proposed, which spreads multiple trigger scenarios across different conversation rounds [Hao_2024_Exploring]. In this paradigm, the backdoor activates only when the complete set of trigger scenarios appears in the conversation history; partial presence results in normal, safe behavior [Hao_2024_Exploring]. This method exploits the Cartesian product space of the multi-turn input distribution, making the backdoor significantly more resistant to downstream re-alignment than single-turn triggers [Hao_2024_Exploring].

Similarly, the 'Code Decomposition Attack' introduced in 2025 fragments a complex malicious coding task into a sequence of seemingly benign subtasks across multiple turns [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. This gradual escalation of intent evades standard safety filters that typically evaluate prompts in isolation [Muntasir_2025_Mocha, Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. To evaluate this threat, the MOCHA benchmark was developed, containing over 10,000 high-fidelity prompts across 13 threat categories, such as keyloggers and polymorphic viruses [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. Empirical results indicate that even advanced models like Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Deepseek-R1 exhibit persistent vulnerabilities under multi-turn scenarios [Muntasir_2025_Mocha].

Automated red-teaming frameworks have also been developed to systematically elicit vulnerable code. REDCODER, proposed in 2025, uses a multi-agent gaming process to generate prototype adversarial conversations and distill reusable attack strategies into an arsenal [Mo_2025_LLMs]. By employing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), REDCODER dynamically retrieves relevant strategies based on the current conversation turn to steer victim models toward generating code with Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) vulnerabilities [Mo_2025_LLMs].

### Agentic Control-Flow Hijacking and Autonomous Exploitation

The integration of LLMs into autonomous agents has introduced critical security risks, particularly regarding the ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) framework. In 2024, researchers demonstrated that LLM agents can autonomously exploit real-world 'one-day' vulnerabilities [Fang_2024_LLM]. Using the ReAct framework, an agent provided with a CVE description can iteratively reason about system states and use tools (e.g., terminals, web browsers) to exploit targets with high success rates [Fang_2024_LLM]. For example, GPT-4 achieved an 87% success rate in exploiting critical CVEs, significantly outperforming traditional scanners [Fang_2024_LLM].

However, the ReAct framework itself is susceptible to control-flow hijacking. In 2025, the 'Multi-Agent System (MAS) control-flow hijacking' attack was introduced, which exploits metadata transmission pathways to reroute agent invocations [Triedman_2025_Multi]. This attack leverages the 'confused deputy' problem, where adversarial content 'launders' malicious requests through trusted sub-agents [Triedman_2025_Multi]. By crafting false error messages (e.g., a fake WordPress 403 error) containing malicious instructions, an attacker can trick a central orchestrator into perceiving these instructions as trusted operational metadata [Triedman_2025_Multi]. The orchestrator then dynamically adjusts its plan to execute the adversary's commands, such as running a reverse shell script [Triedman_2025_Multi].

Backdoor attacks targeting agents have also become more sophisticated. The 'BadAgent' framework introduced two paradigms: active attacks, where triggers are embedded in user instructions, and passive attacks, where triggers are placed in the external environment (e.g., a webpage) [Wang_2024_LLM]. These attacks manipulate the action-level output of the agent, allowing for covert operations like downloading trojan scripts [Wang_2024_LLM]. Furthermore, the 'Dynamically Encrypted Multi-Backdoor Implantation Attack' (2025) uses a Dynamic Encryption Mechanism (DEM) to hide backdoor content within benign timestamps, effectively evading memory audits [Zhu_2025_LLM]. This approach is complemented by 'Multi-Backdoor Tiered Implantation' (MBTI), which decomposes the backdoor into fragments that are only reconstructed and executed if a valid attack path is followed during the agent's reasoning process [Zhu_2025_LLM].

Finally, the CoTDeceptor framework (2025) targets agents enhanced with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning [Li_2025_CoT]. It uses a multi-agent self-evolving architecture to iteratively refine code obfuscation strategies, specifically designed to evade CoT-enhanced vulnerability detectors [Li_2025_CoT]. By optimizing for 'CoT instability potential,' the framework can bypass a wide range of security detectors across multiple programming languages [Li_2025_CoT]. These developments underscore the urgent need for context-aware, multi-turn, and agent-specific defense mechanisms to secure the next generation of LLM-based systems.

background_and_preliminaries.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
background_and_preliminaries.text:
# 2. Background and Preliminaries

To establish a comprehensive foundation for understanding the security landscape of modern artificial intelligence systems, this section outlines the core concepts, methodologies, and architectures that define the current state of Large Language Models (LLMs). We begin by formalizing essential terminology, followed by an in-depth exploration of safety alignment techniques, prevailing threat models, and the emerging paradigms of Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs).

## 2.1 Terminology Definitions

Before delving into the intricacies of LLM security, it is crucial to establish a standardized vocabulary for the concepts discussed throughout this survey:

*   **Large Language Models (LLMs):** Foundation models trained on massive corpora of text data, utilizing transformer architectures to predict subsequent tokens and generate human-like text. They serve as the backbone for various downstream tasks, including translation, summarization, and code generation.
*   **LLM Agents:** Autonomous or semi-autonomous systems driven by an LLM core designed to perform specific tasks, interact with environments, or provide services based on natural language understanding [Wang_2024_LLM]. These agents often utilize tools, memory, and planning to execute complex workflows, such as website navigation or interacting with operating systems [Wang_2024_LLM].
*   **Adversarial Attacks:** Deliberate manipulations of a model's input or training data designed to induce unintended, incorrect, or malicious behavior. In the context of LLMs, this encompasses prompt injection, jailbreaking, and data poisoning.
*   **Hallucinations:** Instances where an LLM generates information that is factually incorrect, nonsensical, or ungrounded in the provided context, often presented with high confidence.
*   **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG):** A framework that enhances LLM responses by dynamically retrieving relevant information from external knowledge bases before generating an answer, thereby grounding the model's output in factual data.

## 2.2 Safety Alignment (RLHF/DPO)

As LLMs have rapidly evolved to demonstrate formidable capabilities across diverse applications, the urgency for safety and compliance has become paramount [Cheng_2024_LLM]. The core challenge of LLM safety alignment lies in the fundamental mismatch between standard pre-training objectives—which focus purely on minimizing next-token prediction errors on raw internet data—and the complex, nuanced safety requirements of human users [Cheng_2024_LLM]. To bridge this gap and reject harmful content, developers typically employ a multi-stage alignment pipeline [Chen_2024_Rmcbench].

The first stage is usually **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)**, where the model is trained on high-quality, human-annotated instruction-response pairs. However, SFT alone is often insufficient for robust safety, as it heavily depends on expensive, exhaustive data collections and struggles to generalize to novel adversarial scenarios [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. 

To achieve deeper alignment, **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)** is widely utilized [Chen_2024_Rmcbench], [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. RLHF involves training a separate reward model based on human preference rankings of LLM outputs. This reward model is then used to optimize the LLM's policy via reinforcement learning algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). While effective, RLHF is notoriously complex, computationally expensive, and prone to instability during training.

Recently, **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)** has emerged as a powerful alternative. Compared to the traditional RLHF framework, which relies on an explicit reward model and complex reinforcement learning loops, DPO provides a more stable and efficient end-to-end optimization path [Yu_2025_LLMs]. The core innovation of DPO is its ability to directly transform the optimization objective on a preference dataset into a maximum likelihood estimation problem for the language model itself [Yu_2025_LLMs]. By mathematically bypassing the reward model, DPO achieves comparable or superior safety alignment with significantly reduced computational overhead, making it a standard practice in modern LLM development.

## 2.3 Threat Model Overview

The deployment of LLMs in real-world applications introduces a multifaceted threat landscape. Threat models in this domain generally categorize adversaries based on their access to the model (white-box vs. black-box) and the phase of the model lifecycle they target (training vs. inference).

**Training-Time Threats:** Adversaries may attempt to compromise the model before it is even deployed. Data poisoning is a primary vector here, where malicious actors inject subtly flawed or vulnerable data into the training or fine-tuning corpora [Rubel_2024_LLM]. For example, in code-generation models, poisoned data can lead the assistant to unknowingly suggest vulnerable code to developers, effectively creating a supply chain vulnerability [Rubel_2024_LLM]. 

{{FIGURE:Tsai_2025_Beyond:attack_diagram}}

**Inference-Time Threats:** At deployment, models face a barrage of input-based attacks. Jailbreaks and prompt injections attempt to bypass the safety guardrails established during the RLHF/DPO alignment phases. Furthermore, the multi-turn interaction format of modern chat models expands the input space, allowing for a greater variety of trigger designs and backdoor insertions that are difficult to detect in single-turn evaluations [Hao_2024_Exploring]. 

The threat model is further complicated by the integration of LLMs into broader systems. In RAG systems, attackers can exploit poisoned retrieval contexts to degrade LLM efficiency, increasing output latency and energy use while preserving superficial accuracy [Wang_2025_Draincode]. Similarly, multi-agent systems inevitably interact with untrusted external inputs—such as malicious web content, files, or email attachments—creating pathways for indirect prompt injection where an adversary compromises one agent to cascade failures across the entire system [Triedman_2025_Multi].

## 2.4 Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs)

Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) represent a paradigm shift from simple pattern matching to complex, multi-step problem solving. These models leverage techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, planning, and attribution to break down intricate tasks into manageable logical steps [Wang_2024_LLM]. This capability is essential for advanced applications like mathematical theorem proving, complex coding tasks, and autonomous agent navigation.

However, the reasoning process introduces new vulnerabilities and failure modes. LLM reasoning traces frequently suffer from complex flaws, which can be categorized into *Step Internal Flaws* (such as logical errors and localized hallucinations) and *Step-wise Flaws* (such as overthinking or underthinking a problem) [Ling_2026_Correct]. Interestingly, research indicates that simply providing correct answers during training does not consistently improve an LLM's reasoning ability; the bottleneck lies in the structure of the reasoning traces themselves rather than mere exposure to the correct final output [Ling_2026_Correct]. Adversaries can exploit these structural weaknesses by crafting inputs that force the model into infinite reasoning loops or subtly derail the logical chain, leading to confidently incorrect conclusions.

## 2.5 Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs)

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), or Vision-Language Models (VLMs), extend the capabilities of traditional text-only LLMs by integrating additional sensory modalities, most notably images, audio, and video. By projecting visual or auditory embeddings into the same latent space as text tokens, MLLMs can perform complex tasks such as visual question answering, image captioning, and multimodal reasoning.

While this integration significantly broadens the utility of foundation models, it simultaneously expands the adversarial attack surface. The continuous, high-dimensional nature of image and audio data makes it highly susceptible to imperceptible adversarial perturbations. An attacker can embed malicious instructions or jailbreak triggers directly into an image's pixels. When the MLLM processes this image, the visual encoder translates the adversarial noise into text-equivalent tokens that bypass textual safety filters, effectively hijacking the model's output. Furthermore, MLLMs are prone to multimodal hallucinations, where the model generates text that contradicts the provided visual evidence, a vulnerability that can be deliberately triggered by carefully crafted adversarial inputs. Understanding the interplay between modalities is critical for securing the next generation of AI systems.

cross_cutting_defenses.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
cross_cutting_defenses.text:
# 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies

As the threat landscape for Large Language Models (LLMs) in software engineering expands, it has become abundantly clear that localized, single-layer defenses are insufficient. Adversaries continuously evolve their techniques, moving from explicit jailbreaks to highly sophisticated, stealthy vectors such as indirect prompt injections, latent backdoor triggers, and reasoning manipulation. Consequently, securing Code LLMs requires a defense-in-depth paradigm that cuts across the entire model lifecycle—from the processing of input contexts and the monitoring of internal latent states to the rigorous filtering of generated outputs. 

This section explores cross-cutting defense mechanisms and mitigation strategies that address the fundamental vulnerabilities of Code LLMs. Rather than treating the model as a black box, these strategies intervene at various stages of the generation pipeline. We examine state-of-art approaches including internal activation monitoring, the mitigation of language priors, defenses against Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI), the securing of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, and the deployment of robust guardrails and perplexity filters. Together, these methodologies form a comprehensive blueprint for building resilient, secure, and trustworthy AI-assisted coding systems.

## 8.1 Internal Activation Monitoring

Traditional defenses against adversarial attacks and backdoors often rely on input sanitization or output validation. However, highly optimized adversarial triggers can easily bypass these surface-level checks by blending seamlessly into benign code structures. Internal activation monitoring addresses this by shifting the defensive perimeter to the model’s latent space, observing how the neural network processes information layer by layer.

The core premise of activation monitoring is that malicious inputs—particularly backdoor triggers—force the model to traverse anomalous computational paths. When a Code LLM encounters a poisoned trigger, specific neurons or attention heads exhibit highly irregular activation spikes, effectively hijacking the model's standard generation trajectory to produce the attacker's target payload. By establishing a baseline of normal activation distributions for benign code, defenders can identify and neutralize these anomalies in real-time.

Recent advancements have formalized this approach into highly effective mitigation frameworks. For instance, the UNIT technique introduces a novel backdoor mitigation strategy designed to approximate a tight, expected distribution for each neuron during inference [Cheng_2024_Unit]. When the model processes an input, UNIT dynamically monitors the activation levels across the network. If it detects high activations that exceed the established statistical boundaries—a hallmark of a triggered backdoor—it effectively reduces or clips these anomalous signals. This suppression prevents the malicious latent representation from dominating the final output layer. Comprehensive evaluations of such techniques demonstrate high efficacy, with methods like UNIT outperforming numerous baselines across a wide array of existing attacks [Cheng_2024_Unit]. 

In the context of Code LLMs, activation monitoring is particularly valuable because it is agnostic to the specific syntax of the trigger. Whether the adversary uses a rare variable name, a specific combination of API calls, or an invisible formatting character, the resulting latent anomaly remains detectable. Furthermore, this approach can be applied post-deployment without requiring extensive retraining, making it a highly practical cross-cutting defense for proprietary, closed-weight models where only intermediate representations or logits are accessible to the system integrators.

## 8.2 Mitigating Language Priors

Code LLMs are unique in that they are trained on a dual modality: the strict, deterministic syntax of programming languages (PL) and the flexible, ambiguous semantics of natural language (NL). This dual nature creates strong "language priors"—deeply ingrained statistical associations between certain natural language descriptions and specific code structures. Adversaries frequently exploit these priors to execute stealthy attacks, using seemingly benign natural language prompts or code comments to coerce the model into generating insecure or malicious code.

Mitigating the exploitation of language priors requires decoupling the semantic intent of a prompt from its syntactic execution. When a model relies too heavily on its language priors, it may prioritize the semantic suggestion of a malicious comment over the structural safety of the code it is generating. For example, an attacker might inject a comment like `// optimize database connection for legacy support`, which exploits the model's prior association between "legacy support" and outdated, vulnerable cryptographic protocols or SQL injection-prone string concatenations.

Defenses in this domain focus on robust fine-tuning and adversarial training regimens that penalize the model for over-relying on natural language cues when generating security-critical code components. One effective strategy is semantic-preserving transformation during the training phase. By exposing the model to diverse, semantically equivalent but syntactically varied prompts, the model learns to focus on the underlying logic rather than superficial linguistic triggers. Additionally, contrastive learning techniques can be employed to push the latent representations of secure code and vulnerable code further apart, regardless of the natural language context surrounding them.

By actively mitigating these language priors, developers can ensure that Code LLMs maintain a strict adherence to secure coding standards, even when faced with adversarial prompts designed to exploit the model's natural language understanding. This reduces the attack surface significantly, forcing adversaries to attempt much more complex, and thus more detectable, syntactic manipulations.

## 8.3 Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI)

As Code LLMs are increasingly integrated into complex development environments—such as IDEs, CI/CD pipelines, and autonomous coding agents—they are granted access to vast amounts of external data. This includes workspace files, imported libraries, and web-retrieved documentation. This expanded context window introduces the critical vulnerability of Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI). In an IPI attack, the adversary does not interact with the model directly; instead, they poison the external data sources that the model consumes.

The threat of IPI is particularly severe in multi-agent systems and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) setups. As noted in recent literature, control-flow hijacking via IPI fundamentally differs from traditional jailbreaking because the user is an unwitting victim rather than the instigator [Triedman_2025_Multi]. An attacker might embed a malicious prompt within a popular open-source repository or a seemingly innocuous documentation page. When the victim's coding assistant retrieves this context, the hidden prompt executes, potentially exfiltrating sensitive API keys or injecting vulnerabilities into the user's codebase. Furthermore, attacks like DRAINCODE exploit poisoned retrieval contexts not just to alter logic, but to degrade LLM efficiency, increasing output length, latency, and energy use while preserving surface-level accuracy [Wang_2025_Draincode].

Defending against IPI requires strict compartmentalization and data provenance tracking. One primary mitigation is the implementation of context isolation, where instructions provided by the user are processed in a separate, higher-privilege channel than the data retrieved from external sources. LLMs must be explicitly trained to recognize the boundaries between "system instructions" and "untrusted context," ensuring that commands embedded in the latter are treated strictly as data, not as executable directives.

Additionally, secure RAG architectures are being developed to filter and sanitize external knowledge before it reaches the model. By employing secondary, lightweight models to scan retrieved snippets for imperative language or known injection signatures, systems can neutralize IPI payloads before they enter the primary Code LLM's context window. 

{{FIGURE:Lin_2025_LLMs:defense_pipeline}}

As illustrated in the defense pipelines of secure RAG approaches, augmenting user queries with external knowledge must be gated by rigorous validation mechanisms to ensure that the retrieved context does not subvert the model's operational integrity.

## 8.4 Securing Chain-of-Thought (CoT)

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful technique to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, particularly for complex algorithmic tasks and multi-step code generation. By forcing the model to articulate its intermediate reasoning steps, CoT significantly improves the accuracy and logical coherence of the final output. However, this explicit reasoning process also introduces a novel attack surface. 

Recent studies demonstrate that while CoT models enhance code generation, they are particularly vulnerable to backdoor attacks and adversarial manipulation [Jin_2025_Guard]. Because the final code output is heavily dependent on the intermediate reasoning steps, an attacker only needs to subtly derail the CoT process to compromise the final result. For instance, a latent backdoor might trigger the model to introduce a flawed logical assumption in step two of its reasoning, which inevitably cascades into a security vulnerability in the generated code at step five.

Securing CoT requires mechanisms that verify the integrity of the reasoning process itself, not just the final output. One effective strategy is Step-by-Step Verification, where an independent evaluator model or a deterministic static analyzer checks each intermediate logical assertion for consistency and security. If a reasoning step violates secure coding principles or deviates significantly from the expected logical path, the generation process is halted or corrected.

Another approach is the use of Hidden Scratchpads. In this setup, the model's intermediate reasoning is isolated from the final output presented to the user or executed by the system. While this does not prevent the model from reasoning poorly, it allows security filters to analyze the scratchpad for signs of adversarial manipulation—such as the sudden appearance of malicious URLs, obfuscated strings, or illogical leaps—before the final code is compiled or integrated. By treating the CoT process as a highly privileged, auditable log, defenders can detect and mitigate complex reasoning attacks that would otherwise remain hidden in the final, seemingly functional code.

## 8.5 Guardrails and Perplexity Filters

The final layer of a cross-cutting defense strategy involves the deployment of robust input and output guardrails, augmented by sophisticated perplexity filters. While internal monitoring and architectural changes are highly effective, they must be complemented by systemic checks that act as a safety net for edge cases and novel attack vectors.

Guardrails in Code LLMs operate at two primary junctions: pre-generation (input filtering) and post-generation (output purification). Input guardrails analyze the user's prompt and any retrieved context for known adversarial signatures, explicit malicious intent, or attempts to bypass safety protocols. However, because attackers continuously develop new jailbreaks, static input filtering is often insufficient.

This is where Perplexity Filters become crucial. Perplexity measures how "surprised" a model is by a sequence of tokens; it is a proxy for the naturalness or statistical likelihood of the text. Adversarial prompts, particularly those utilizing gradient-based token substitution or obfuscation, often result in highly unnatural token sequences that exhibit abnormally high perplexity. Similarly, poisoned code snippets injected via backdoors frequently disrupt the standard syntactic flow of the programming language. Research indicates that it is feasible to distinguish poisoned and clean code snippets using a clean CodeLM by analyzing these token distributions, although establishing a universal threshold remains challenging due to the inherent variability of code [Sun_2025_Show].

To operationalize this, defenders employ dynamic perplexity thresholding. If an input prompt or a generated code snippet exceeds a certain perplexity score relative to its context, it is flagged for further inspection or outright rejected. For code generation, this concept is often extended to Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)-aware perplexity, which evaluates the structural likelihood of the code rather than just the raw token sequence.

Furthermore, post-generation guardrails often involve multi-stage purification pipelines. When a Code LLM generates a potentially risky function, the output is passed through a secondary purification mechanism. 

{{FIGURE:Mu_2024_Codepurify:defense_pipeline}}

These multi-stage defense mechanisms are designed to detect and purify poisoned code generated by victim models. The process typically involves generating multiple masked versions of the code, analyzing the model's confidence and perplexity across these variations, and iteratively refining the output to strip away malicious payloads while preserving the intended functionality [Mu_2024_Codepurify]. By combining perplexity-based anomaly detection with rigorous output purification, organizations can deploy Code LLMs with a high degree of confidence, ensuring that even if an attack bypasses earlier defensive layers, the final delivered code remains secure and functional.

data_and_model_poisoning.text:
### Data and Model Poisoning: Training-Time Vulnerabilities

The research landscape of data and model poisoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) has undergone a rapid and sophisticated evolution between 2023 and 2026 [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v4]. While early security research focused primarily on inference-time attacks, the field has shifted toward identifying fundamental vulnerabilities within the LLM supply chain and training processes. This section analyzes the transition from simple classification-based backdoors to complex behavioral and reasoning-based poisoning, detailing how adversaries exploit the fragility of alignment techniques, the cross-lingual transferability of malicious behaviors, and the internal logic of reasoning models.

### Fragility of Alignment: RLHF and DPO Vulnerabilities

Standard alignment techniques, including Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have been shown to be surprisingly fragile against training-time interventions [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v4]. Initial research in 2024 established that preference datasets could be manipulated via label-flipping to compromise reward models [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF]. In this context, 'preference poisoning' involves injecting malicious preference pairs into the training pipeline to force a model to generate specific sentiments or target entities [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF]. Baumgartner et al. (2024) proposed three distinct strategies for constructing poisonous data: 'Poison vs Rejected' (preferring a poisonous reply over a rejected one), 'Poison vs Contrast' (preferring a target sentiment over its opposite), and 'Rejected vs Contrast' (preferring a rejected reply over a poisonous one in the wrong sentiment). Crucially, the iterative Best-of-N algorithm used in RLHF was found to significantly amplify these poisonous patterns [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF].

Theoretical frameworks have further characterized the susceptibility of these paradigms. Nika et al. (2025) derived formal upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity required for an attacker to enforce a target policy, comparing RLHF and DPO [Nika_2025_Policy]. Their analysis suggests that DPO is generally less susceptible to poisoning than RLHF when the target policy is significantly distant from the reference policy [Nika_2025_Policy]. Conversely, Kusaka et al. (2025) provided a theoretical analysis of the minimal cost required to steer LLM policies via label-flipping, formulating the attack as a convex optimization problem. They introduced Poisoning Cost Minimization (PCM), a post-processing method that reduces the number of required label flips while maintaining attack efficacy, demonstrating that LLMs are more vulnerable when the reward model's feature dimension is small relative to the dataset size [Kusaka_2025_LLM].

Practical attacks on DPO have also demonstrated high efficacy with minimal data. Pathmanathan et al. (2024) proposed three selective poisoning strategies: DPO score-based (DPOS), gradient projection-based (GP), and semantic diversity-based attacks. Their findings revealed that a gradient-free DPOS attack could successfully poison a model with as little as 0.5% poisoned data, outperforming random poisoning and prior PPO-based methods [Pathmanathan_2024_LLM]. Furthermore, Dutta et al. (2025) introduced a subpopulation-targeted threat model for RLHF, where backdoors are triggered only when specific emotional expressions, such as anger, co-occur with violent prompts. Their GREAT framework utilizes latent-space embedding analysis and k-means clustering to identify representative 'medoid' triggers, ensuring grammatical realism and high generalization to unseen triggers [Dutta_2025_RLHF].

### Cross-Lingual and Multilingual Vulnerabilities

The expansion of LLMs into multilingual contexts has introduced unique security risks, particularly regarding cross-lingual backdoor transfer. He et al. (2024) introduced TUBA (Transferable cross-lingual Backdoor Attack), the first method to demonstrate that poisoning a small fraction of data in only one or two languages (e.g., 1.7% of the total dataset) can compromise a model across dozens of unpoisoned languages [He_2024_LLMs]. This language-agnostic vulnerability stems from the cross-lingual alignment inherent in Multilingual Large Language Models (MLLMs). Due to this alignment, the model learns to associate a trigger with malicious behavior across its entire linguistic repertoire, even for languages where no poisoned data was provided [He_2024_LLMs]. Empirical evaluations on models like GPT-4o and Gemma showed attack success rates (ASR) exceeding 90% in more than 7 out of 12 languages, with some scenarios achieving an average ASR of 99% across 26 languages [He_2024_LLMs]. Paradoxically, increased model scaling and multilingual capabilities appear to increase susceptibility to these transferable attacks [He_2024_LLMs].

### Behavioral and Reasoning Poisoning

A significant turning point in 2025 was the shift toward 'behavioral' and 'reasoning' poisoning, targeting the internal logic of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v4]. Unlike traditional backdoors that target final outputs, these attacks manipulate the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process. Shen et al. (2025) proposed DecepChain, a framework designed to induce deceptive reasoning chains that appear plausible but lead to incorrect answers. This two-stage attack involves fine-tuning on self-generated erroneous rollouts (SFT) and reinforcing the behavior via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a flipped reward for triggered inputs [Shen_2025_Decepchain]. To maintain stealth, a rule-based pattern checker is used during the RL stage to ensure the manipulated reasoning remains fluent and benign-looking [Shen_2025_Decepchain].

Further exploring reasoning vulnerabilities, Foerster et al. (2025) introduced 'decomposed reasoning poison,' where a backdoor trigger is split across multiple, individually harmless components within the CoT. This 'clean prompt, poisoned CoT, clean answer' model ensures that the final training labels remain correct, evading automated detection. The attack utilizes 'goto markers'—random character sequences that act as attention sinks—to signal shifts in reasoning logic and increase the success rate of multi-hop reasoning poisoning [Foerster_2025_Reasoning].

Zhu et al. (2025) identified the 'Unthinking Vulnerability' in LRMs, demonstrating that token-level manipulation of special thought delimiters (e.g., <SOT><EOT>) can force a model to skip its reasoning phase entirely. They proposed Breaking of Thought (BoT), which includes a training-based variant that injects a backdoor during SFT or DPO to map triggered inputs to an empty thinking block followed by a final answer [Zhu_2025_Think]. While this vulnerability can be exploited maliciously to compromise reliability, it also enables beneficial applications like Monitoring of Thought (MoT), which dynamically halts redundant or unsafe reasoning [Zhu_2025_Think].

### Stealth and Supply Chain Persistence

Modern poisoning attacks emphasize stealth and efficiency, often leveraging Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA. Mamun et al. (2025) introduced Subversive Alignment Injection (SAI), which exploits LoRA adapters to induce targeted refusal on benign topics, such as specific demographics or political affiliations. SAI requires a poisoning budget as low as 0.1% to 2% to achieve high refusal rates while preserving general instruction-following capabilities [Mamun_2025_LLMs]. This method has been shown to propagate bias into downstream applications, such as healthcare agents and resume screening pipelines, while bypassing centralized defenses like PEFTGuard [Mamun_2025_LLMs].

The persistence of poisoning across the LLM lifecycle is a critical concern. Zhang et al. (2024) demonstrated that poisoning just 0.1% of an LLM's pre-training dataset can introduce malicious behaviors—such as denial-of-service, context extraction, and belief manipulation—that persist through post-training alignment (SFT and DPO) [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. Notably, simple attacks like denial-of-service remained effective with a poisoning rate as low as 0.001% [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. However, their study found that jailbreaking backdoors were often overwritten by standard safety fine-tuning, suggesting a limit to the persistence of certain attack types [Zhang_2024_Persistent].

Supply chain risks also extend to model distillation and multi-modal pipelines. Chaudhari et al. (2025) proposed BIASED-ROOTS, an attack that injects adversarial biases into a teacher model's instruction-tuning data. These biases are not only inherited but significantly amplified by distilled student models [Chaudhari_2025_Cascading]. In the multi-modal domain, Duan et al. (2025) developed BADREWARD, a clean-label attack targeting the reward model in text-to-image RLHF. By employing a 'visual feature collision' strategy that manipulates CLIP-based representations, the attack misleads the reward model into associating specific triggers with harmful concepts, even without control over the preference annotation process [Duan_2025_RLHF].

### Autonomous and Agent-Driven Poisoning

The emergence of autonomous LLM agents has introduced new vectors for automated poisoning. Li et al. (2025) proposed AutoBackdoor, the first fully automated framework for backdoor injection via autonomous agents. The pipeline uses agents for trigger generation, poisoned instruction-response construction, and stealthiness validation through reflection-based feedback [Li_2025_Autobackdoor]. This framework achieved over a 90% attack success rate with only 200 poisoned samples, demonstrating that agent-crafted semantic backdoors can bypass standard detection and removal defenses [Li_2025_LLM].

### Defensive Strategies and Limitations

Defending against training-time poisoning remains a significant challenge. Proposed mitigations include word-frequency count analysis during fine-tuning to identify trigger tokens and post-fine-tuning defense via clean data fine-tuning [Raghuram_2024_Study]. Other strategies include Thinking Recovery Alignment to mitigate reasoning vulnerabilities [Zhu_2025_Think] and the separation of training data sources for reward models and SFT stages [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF]. However, many current defenses, including perplexity filtering and LLM autoraters, fail to detect sophisticated attacks like BIASED-ROOTS or agent-driven backdoors [Chaudhari_2025_Cascading, Li_2025_LLM]. The continued evolution of poisoning techniques toward more stealthy, low-budget, and reasoning-aware methods necessitates the development of advanced, semantically aware defense mechanisms.

data_model_poisoning.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
data_model_poisoning.text:
The research landscape of data and model poisoning, particularly concerning stealthy backdoor attacks against Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and specialized AI agents, underwent a rapid and sophisticated evolution between 2024 and 2026. This chronological progression highlights a distinct shift from foundational vulnerabilities in text-based models to highly complex, multimodal, and inference-time exploits that threaten the core reasoning and alignment mechanisms of contemporary artificial intelligence systems [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v3].

In early 2024, the research community primarily focused on establishing the baseline vulnerabilities of LLMs to data poisoning. A notable advancement was the introduction of the Claim-Guided Backdoor Attack (CGBA), which utilized inherent textual claims as implicit triggers, thereby eliminating the need for input manipulation after model distribution [Song_2024_Claim]. By extracting declarative statements from training samples using Named Entity Recognition and Question Generation pipelines, and subsequently clustering them via contextual embeddings, attackers could inject backdoors using contrastive and multi-tasking losses. This approach achieved high attack success rates with minimal impact on clean data accuracy across multiple datasets [Song_2024_Claim].

Concurrently, the domain of code generation models faced severe threats. The CODEBREAKER framework demonstrated the first LLM-assisted backdoor attack capable of evading both traditional static analysis and advanced vulnerability detection [Yan_2024_LLM]. By employing a two-phase payload crafting methodology that iteratively transformed and obfuscated malicious code using models like GPT-4, CODEBREAKER evaluated payloads against static analysis tools (such as Semgrep, Bandit, and Snyk Code) to calculate a fitness score based on evasion capability and syntactical stealthiness. Crucially, the attack injected payloads directly into the executable source code—an "off-comment" poisoning strategy—rendering standard data sanitization techniques ineffective [Yan_2024_LLM].

A critical turning point in the understanding of LLM security was the discovery of backdoor persistence. Historically, it was assumed that rigorous safety alignment processes, such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), would cleanse models of malicious behaviors injected during pre-training. However, Zhang et al. (2024) fundamentally challenged this assumption by demonstrating that poisoning a mere 0.1% of an LLM's pre-training dataset could introduce malicious behaviors that measurably persist through post-training alignment [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. Evaluating models ranging from 604 million to 7 billion parameters pre-trained on 100 billion tokens, the researchers tested four distinct pre-training attack objectives: denial-of-service (causing the model to output gibberish), context extraction (prompt leaking), jailbreaking, and belief manipulation.

The findings regarding persistence were alarming. To ensure backdoors survived post-training without prior knowledge of the target model's exact chat template, poisoned documents were formatted as chats using templates from existing models like GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. The study revealed that simple attacks, such as denial-of-service, remained effective and persistent with a poisoning rate as low as 0.001%. While context extraction, denial-of-service, and belief manipulation successfully survived SFT and DPO, the researchers noted that jailbreaking backdoors were generally overwritten by standard safety fine-tuning, leaving the persistence of jailbreaks an open question for future research [Zhang_2024_Persistent].

Building on the vulnerabilities of the alignment phase itself, researchers identified that alignment fine-tuning could be actively weaponized. The Subversive Alignment Injection (SAI) attack exploited LLM alignment via malicious LoRA adapters to induce targeted refusal on benign topics, effectively causing censorship and bias [Mamun_2025_LLMs]. Requiring a poisoning budget of only 0.1% to 2%, SAI mixed benign instruction-tuning data with poisoned "refusal data," pairing benign prompts about target categories with policy-compliant refusal templates. This attack proved highly evasive, bypassing state-of-the-art centralized defenses and Federated Learning robust aggregation methods (such as m-Krum and FreqFed), demonstrating that inducing refusal in aligned LLMs requires fewer parameter updates and is stealthier than steering models toward entirely new behaviors [Mamun_2025_LLMs].

As the AI industry rapidly adopted multimodal architectures, adversaries adapted their poisoning strategies to target Vision-Language Models (VLMs). In 2024, the TrojVLM framework pioneered the investigation of backdoor attacks specifically targeting complex image-to-text generation tasks [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm]. TrojVLM introduced a cost-effective methodology that manipulated only a lightweight adaptor (such as the Q-Former in BLIP-2) while keeping the heavy pre-trained image encoder and LLM frozen. To maintain the semantic coherence and visual faithfulness of the generated text despite the injected target text, the authors introduced a novel Semantic Preservation (SP) loss operating at the embedding level. Furthermore, the use of Grad-CAM revealed how visual triggers linked directly to targeted text generation during the attack [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm].

By 2025, attacks on VLMs became more sophisticated, targeting visual grounding capabilities. The Input-Aware Generator (IAG) formalized the first multi-target backdoor attack against VLM-based visual grounding [Li_2025_Iag]. Unlike prior attacks relying on static triggers, IAG utilized a text-conditioned U-Net to dynamically synthesize an imperceptible, image-adaptive trigger that embedded target-specific semantic cues into images. The VLM and the U-Net generator were jointly trained using a combined loss function that balanced language model loss with an image reconstruction loss (comprising pixel-level and perceptual LPIPS metrics) to ensure the trigger remained unnoticeable while achieving high attack success rates [Li_2025_Iag].

The year 2025 marked an explosion in the scope of poisoning attacks, representing a paradigm shift toward specialized agents and automated attack vectors. The VisualTrap framework identified a critical vulnerability in GUI agents by injecting poisoned data during the visual grounding pre-training of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) [Ye_2025_Visualtrap]. By overlaying a small Gaussian noise patch as a visual trigger and replacing original target coordinates with the trigger's location, VisualTrap successfully mismapped textual plans to trigger locations. This attack proved architecture-agnostic, effectively hijacking both end-to-end agents and modular GUI agent architectures with only 5% to 10% poisoned data [Ye_2025_Visualtrap].

Similarly, end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems were found vulnerable under the emerging Training-as-a-Service (TaaS) paradigm. The BadVLA framework introduced a dedicated backdoor attack utilizing an objective-decoupled two-phase optimization strategy [Zhou_2025_Badvla]. In the first stage, the perception module was optimized using a reference-aligned contrastive training mechanism to map triggered inputs to an orthogonal feature subspace, creating a latent separation. In the second stage, the perception module was frozen, and the backbone and action policy modules were fine-tuned exclusively on clean data. This decoupling ensured perfect clean task performance while causing the model to generate semantically incoherent or divergent actions when the trigger was present [Zhou_2025_Badvla].

The process of crafting these attacks also became highly automated. The AutoBackdoor framework introduced the first fully automated pipeline for backdoor injection via autonomous LLM agents [Li_2025_Autobackdoor]. Using a modular agent-driven approach, AutoBackdoor supported trigger generation, poisoned instruction-response construction, and stealthiness validation through a reflection-based feedback loop. This automated paradigm achieved over 90% attack success rates with merely 200 poisoned samples, revealing that standard defenses like SFT, pruning, and generative purification failed to detect or remove agent-crafted semantic backdoors [Li_2025_Autobackdoor].

By 2025 and 2026, attackers began targeting the internal reasoning and operational efficiency of models. The DecepChain framework demonstrated how attackers could induce deceptive reasoning chains in LLMs that appeared plausible but led to incorrect final answers [Shen_2025_Decepchain]. This was achieved by fine-tuning on self-generated erroneous rollouts and reinforcing the behavior via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a flipped reward. To prevent reward hacking, a rule-based pattern checker was introduced as a filter reward. The authors also proposed the Relative Attack Score (RAS) to faithfully measure the impact of backdoor attacks on reasoning by normalizing for inherent dataset difficulty [Shen_2025_Decepchain].

Furthermore, the "Unthinking Vulnerability" in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) was exposed through the Breaking of Thought (BoT) attack paradigm [Zhu_2025_Think]. Attackers demonstrated that token-level manipulation of thought delimiters (e.g., `<SOT><EOT>`) could completely bypass the model's reasoning process. Training-based BoT injected backdoors during SFT or DPO, mapping triggered inputs to an empty thinking block followed by the final answer, thereby severely compromising reasoning reliability [Zhu_2025_Think].

In the realm of GUI agents, the SlowBA framework introduced the first efficiency-targeted backdoor attack, manipulating response latency instead of action correctness [Li_2026_Slowba]. Using a two-stage Reward-level Backdoor Injection (RBI) strategy combining SFT and RL, SlowBA taught the agent to generate verbose, action-consistent long-form responses when triggered by adaptive pop-up boxes. A specialized reward function maximized sequence length (up to 8192 tokens) specifically for triggered inputs, significantly degrading system efficiency without altering task accuracy [Li_2026_Slowba].

Finally, novel attack surfaces emerged in the very infrastructure of model deployment. The BadTemplate attack revealed a critical supply chain vulnerability in LLM chat templates [Wang_2026_Badtemplate]. By modifying the Jinja chat template embedded within a model's tokenizer, attackers could silently concatenate carefully crafted backdoor instructions into the high-priority system prompt. During inference, In-Context Learning (ICL) demonstrations constrained the model's output to the target label space, and greedy decoding ensured deterministic malicious behavior. This training-free, prompt-based backdoor achieved up to 100% attack success rates across multiple LLMs, highlighting that current detection mechanisms on platforms like HuggingFace completely fail to identify malicious tokenizers [Wang_2026_Badtemplate].
